beit_shmuel.en:
(א) And give it to the agent. In the Talmud, Rava asked: if he said, and give it to the agent, what is the law? Rashi explained: if they gave it to the agent and it was later lost, do we say they have already fulfilled their agency? It further states: Ravina said to Rav Ashi, if he said, and give it to the agent, and he shall bring it, what is the law? Rashi explained: if you say that when he did not say and he shall bring it, they have already fulfilled their agency, nevertheless if he said and he shall bring it, one may say they have not fulfilled their agency until the Get reaches her hand, and that is why he concluded and said and he shall bring it. Ri"v wrote regarding Rashi's words, who explained the question as where it was lost, that the same applies if it was found invalid. Rambam wrote if it was found invalid, and the same applies if it was lost. Beit Yosef challenged him and wrote that according to Rambam the Talmud's question is specifically if it was found invalid, for one may say that since their obligation was only to give it to the agent, even if they gave an invalid Get they fulfilled their agency; but if it was a valid Get and they gave it to the agent and it was lost, he did not ask, and they certainly fulfilled their agency. If they wrote another Get, the Get is void. At first glance it appears that Ri"v, Rashi, and Rambam do not disagree. When Rambam wrote and it was found invalid, he means that after they gave it to the agent a defect was found in it that occurred in the Get after delivery, which is like being lost. Likewise, according to Rashi, who explained if it was lost, the same applies if it was found invalid. But if the invalidity existed before delivery, they do not disagree, and according to all opinions they did not fulfill their agency, as the Tur wrote. This is also the Maggid Mishneh's intent when he wrote if it was found invalid or lost: he asks about invalidity after delivery, but if it was invalid from the outset, according to all opinions they may write another Get. In any event, it is explicit from the Maggid Mishneh that if it was a valid Get and was lost, that too is the question, unlike Beit Yosef, who wrote that if it was valid and lost there is no question and they certainly fulfilled their agency. If he did not say and he shall bring it, the law is not explicit here. The Tur wrote that they certainly were not made agents. Beit Yosef wrote that although he wrote certainly, his intent is only that it is doubtful, because the question was not resolved. Even though the second question was stated in the form if you say, and the Geonim rule according to an if you say, nevertheless since the if you say is not explicit, no one rules according to it. According to what I wrote in Choshen Mishpat siman 346, that the Rosh does not rule according to the approach of the Geonim, this was unnecessary. See further below in siman 137, and see Rambam chapter 7 of Hilkhot Nachalot, chapter 2 of Hilkhot Sheluachin, and chapter 8 law 3. In Taz he wrote that the Tur holds that in the first question they certainly fulfilled their agency, and what Ravina said to Rav Ashi, what if he said and he shall bring it to her, means that he told him Rava did not ask when he did not say and he shall bring it; rather, specifically when he said and he shall bring it did he ask. For practical halakhah, the main ruling is that even if he did not say and he shall bring it, it is still doubtful. Beit Yosef wrote at the end of seif 7 that perhaps Rambam explains the first question as whether they can give the Get themselves to the woman: even though he appointed another agent, nevertheless he did not remove them from the agency. This is Rif's approach. In the novellae of Rabbi Shelomo Kohen on the eight chapters of Hilkhot Gittin, he wrote that Rambam's words in chapter 9 law 31 escaped Beit Yosef's attention, for there Rambam writes that there is no doubt in the matter and he cannot be his agent. Although there he wrote if he said and he shall bring it, there is no reason to distinguish. See siman 141.

turei_zahav.en:
(א) And he shall bring it to her. In the Gemara Rava asked Rav Nachman: if one said, "Write it and give it to the agent," and it was lost before they gave it to her, what is the law? Have they removed themselves, because we say they have performed their agency, or was he concerned only for their exertion? Rashi explains that even here, until the get reaches her hand and she is divorced, he made them agents to write, but he was concerned not to trouble them with the delivery. Ravina said to Rav Ashi: if he said, "and he shall bring it to her," what is the law? Rashi explains: if you say that where he said only "write and give it to the agent," and they wrote and gave it to him, then if it was lost they have performed their agency, for they completed all that he commanded, what is the law here? Do we say that since he said, "write and give it to the agent and he shall bring it to her," he made them agents to write again until it reaches her hand, or is there no difference? The question remains unresolved. The Tur writes that if he told the scribe, "write and give it to the agent," and it was lost from the agent, certainly he made them agents only to bring it to the agent. Even if he said "and he shall bring it," we do not say he made them agents until it is brought; once they gave it to the agent they performed their agency, and they may not write another get until they ask him. If they wrote another and she was divorced with it, she is doubtfully divorced. But if they wrote an invalid get and gave it to the agent, they certainly may write another. His words show that regarding Rava's question he rules that it certainly is not a get, while regarding Ravina's question he rules that it is doubtful. This is difficult: why should we not also treat the first case as doubtful? Beit Yosef wrote that the Tur's statement that it is doubtful also refers to the first case.
Words of the glossator: Beit Shmuel, s.k. 7, wrote that according to what he wrote in Choshen Mishpat siman 346, that the Rosh did not rule according to the geonim, he would not need this. Taz wrote that the Tur holds that in the first question they certainly performed their agency, and that Ravina's question of "and he shall bring it" means that Rava's question was specifically in a case where that phrase was said. In practice, however, even where he did not say "and he shall bring it," it is also a doubt. The glossator notes that Taz had already anticipated the point about Choshen Mishpat, and he strengthens the words of his grandfather, Taz: the precision is that the Gemara does not say "Ravina asked Rav Ashi," but rather that Ravina said to Rav Ashi, indicating that he was clarifying Rava's original question. Even so, one might explain that Ravina was asking what Rava would hold if "and he shall bring it" had been said. Therefore the issue remains one of analysis, but for halachah there is strong ground to treat even the first case as doubtful.
(ב) And the get is found void, etc. This is Rambam's language, and Beit Yosef explains that if it was lost, they have performed their agency, since it was valid. In my humble opinion this is not so. If the phrase "and he shall bring it" has power to extend the agency until it reaches her hand, then the same should apply where it was lost, since it was still within the time of the agency. Therefore this too should be doubtful where he said "and he shall bring it." Rambam did not specifically use "void" or "invalid" because the Gemara there discusses that case, where the name was written incorrectly; but for the practical law the same principle applies. The dispute with Rambam is only where he said "and he shall bring it" and the get was found invalid: according to the Tur they may write another, and this is the "some say" brought by Rama.
